title: Python from Scratch
text:
Most programming tutorials start by having you type something and promising it will make sense later. That works for some people. For everyone else it produces a year of copying code that runs without any idea why.
This series takes the other route. The first three pages are foundations and contain no Python at all — they are about what a programming language is, what a computer is physically doing when it runs one, and how to pick a language in the first place. Once that is in place, the syntax stops being arbitrary and starts being obvious.

title: Choosing a Programming Language
text:
Python is my language of choice. But in my opinion, choosing which language to start with is far less important than simply starting.
Moving between programming languages means learning new words, sure. It does not mean relearning how computers handle information. The logic underneath computer science is essentially a form of math, and concepts like multiplication and addition work just fine even if we change bases or change how we write them down.

title: Choosing a Programming Language
section: An example of what actually changes
text:
An example of what actually changes
Python makes a lot of assumptions for you. If you want to store a number to use later, you tell it x = 5 and it runs without complaint. Python sees a whole number on its own and assumes it is an integer1. It handles the memory and the background categorisation for you.
C does not make the same assumptions. Put x = 5 into C and it breaks. C assumes nothing about what x is supposed to be, so it has no idea how much memory to give it. You need to say explicitly that x is an integer:
int x = 5;
And then it handles it no problem.
The logic of storing and manipulating data is the same in both cases. The language used to describe it changed. Learning the logic of computers is usually the hardest part for people, and transitioning to another language afterwards is nowhere near as difficult.
That said, the language you begin with often goes hand in hand with what you want to accomplish. Here is the honest version of the trade-offs.

title: Choosing a Programming Language
text:
So which one?
Do you want to work in data analysis or AI? Python.
Game development? C++ or C#.
Do you want to understand the ins and outs of how a computer handles information? C.
Do you want to hang with the old computational physicists and complain about how slow Python is? Fortran.
Full-stack or web development? JavaScript/TypeScript.
A phone app? Java.
Rust and Go are new enough that I honestly don’t know much about them, but if you want to dive into that territory, go for it.






And if you don’t know what you want to do yet, I will make it simple: start with Python. Then go to Lesson 1.

title: What Is a Programming Language?
text: Think of writing code as providing an explicit set of instructions to a computer. The programming language is an interpreter that takes those instructions and translates them into something the computer can understand. A programming language, in many ways, is exactly that — a language. It has its own syntax, grammar, and vocabulary.

title: What Is a Programming Language?
section: Learn the language, or hire a translator
text:
Learn the language, or hire a translator
Let’s say you speak English, but you want to communicate with someone who speaks Chinese. There needs to be some way for the two of you to understand each other.
One possibility is to learn Chinese well enough to say whatever you need to. That takes a very long time and quite a bit of study. The equivalent for talking to a computer is not learning Chinese — it is learning to flip bits on and off and speak in binary. Binary has a structure very different from most spoken and written languages, so that route is an even greater challenge.
The other possibility is to find someone who already speaks Chinese and ask them to translate for you. The catch is that this translator doesn’t understand English perfectly. They understand it in a way that is very literal and very basic. They have no mind of their own to read between the lines, catch connotation, or infer what you meant. To communicate, you have to be exact about the words you choose.






It might help to think of a programming language as a child that is only capable of doing things you have taught it to do.



Want it to know what a banana is? You have to teach it what a banana is. Want it to write its own name? Teach it to write its name. Want it to solve a complicated problem? Teach it how to solve the problem.
The advantage of a language like Python is that other people have already figured out how to teach it a great many useful things, and you get to use their work. I am not going to spend my afternoon explaining to Python, in its own terms, how to compute a logarithm. I am going to import NumPy, because somebody else already did.

title: What Is a Programming Language?
text:
A worked example: the sandwich
Let’s watch what happens when we tell this computer translator to “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.”
The translator will attempt to recognise each word, because literal translation is the only thing it can do:


make — might already be associated with a function like “to create.”
a — a simple word referring to a singular object. Easy syntax to recognise.
peanut — might already be associated with a type of data or object.
butter — might already have a match in memory.
butter — may take on a property away from its default definition, based on context.
peanut combined with butter — recognised as a specific object, “peanut butter.”
and — a simple logical operator that brings two concepts together.
jelly — might already have an association in memory.
sandwich — not defined. It has never learned what a sandwich is.


The translator breaks. It does not know what to do, because it does not know what a “sandwich” is. If it is well built, it throws an error:
Error: I don't know what 'sandwich' is.
Which is the translator’s way of saying: if you want this statement translated, you need to explicitly define “sandwich” first.

Defining a sandwich
So we have to define a sandwich in terms it can already handle. Something like sandwich = food between 2 slices of bread.
The translator processes the new definition:


= tells the translator we are defining a new term.
food is recognised as a broad category of edible items.
between is recognised as a positional relationship.
2 is easy — the translator is very good with numbers.
slices is recognised as a term describing parts of something.
of gives the dependent relationship between two things.
bread is an object it already knows.
The of instructs it to connect “slices” and “bread” into “slices of bread.”
The 2 now fixes the exact integer quantity of slices.
between combines the “food” with the “2 slices of bread.”
It stores in memory that “sandwich” means “food between 2 slices of bread.”




Running it again
Now we can attempt the original statement a second time: “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.”


make triggers the creation function.
a sets the quantity to 1.
peanut butter is recognised as a specific ingredient.
and links ingredients together.
jelly is recognised as a specific ingredient.
sandwich is now recognised as the structure “food between 2 slices of bread.”
The linked food is placed into the required position of the structure.
The whole thing compiles into absolute, literal machine code.
The computer executes the machine code and makes a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.


Python, C++, Fortran and the rest are all simply translators. Each has its own syntax and rules tied to very specific computer translations, and you can only work inside the framework of the translation it offers.

title: What Is a Programming Language?
section: A note on AI and vibe-coding
text:
A note on AI and vibe-coding
The rise of vibe-coding1 has tried to circumvent all of this. Unfortunately, at its core, the vast majority of vibe-coding just inserts another translator into the chain. You tell an AI model what you are trying to do, that model translates your objective into code, and the computer’s translator turns that code into machine instructions.
This can be genuinely useful — it means you do not have to learn a new programming language to get something built. But it also puts one more system between you and the computer. In the translator analogy, you have hired a second translator who speaks great English and is very good at talking to the first translator.
The system works, but it is bounded by two things at once: your ability to communicate with the AI model, and the model’s ability to communicate with both you and the computer. As long as the model is better at this than you are, it lets you build things beyond your current technical ability. The problem is that if you rely on it completely, you will never be able to work beyond the model’s ability to translate for you. Worse, the natural learning process recentres on learning how to interact with AI models, which is time not spent learning the core logic of a programming language.
It is also worth remembering that most of these models are controlled by corporations who can change them at any time. They can get worse, become restricted, or move behind a steeper paywall.






TipThe short version



If you are going to use AI models to help write code, approach it as “How do I do this?” rather than “Do this for me.” The first keeps you connected to the concepts at every skill level. The second builds a dependency you cannot see until it fails.

title: Teaching Philosophy
text:
I believe any student can learn from the right teacher.
I have had many, many conversations with students whose biggest struggle came down to a disconnect between them and their instructor. Not ability, not effort — a mismatch in how the two of them were carving up the world.
The relationship often reminds me of Plato’s cave. The teacher is trying to bring the student into the teacher’s world, but the student can only see that world through the lens of their own. Every step forward is a small breach in how the student already understands things, and the wrong guide will struggle to help them through it.
What my own teaching has taught me is that the arrow runs both directions. The teacher is also only capable of interpreting the world from inside their own perspective, and the student is also, constantly, trying to pull the teacher into theirs. Perhaps that is just an analogy for communication in general. But it strikes me as an apt description of the specific difficulty of being both the teacher and the student at once. Both are captives of their own viewpoint.
That framing changes what the job is. If the gap is a translation problem, then the work is not repeating the explanation louder — it is finding out which language the student already speaks and building the explanation out of that. A student who understands how a bank account works already understands conservation laws. A student who has argued with an autocorrect already understands most of what makes a compiler frustrating. The material is rarely the obstacle. The route in is.

title: Teaching Philosophy
section: What that looks like in practice
text:
What that looks like in practice
I ask what you already know before I tell you anything. Not to grade it — to find the bridge.
I make the reasoning visible, including the dead ends. Textbooks show the path that worked, which quietly implies that the author saw it immediately. They didn’t. Showing the false starts is more honest and more useful.
I refuse to call anything trivial. “Obviously” and “simply” are words that tell a struggling student the problem is them.
I let the student be wrong out loud. A misconception you can see is one I can work with. One you are hiding because you are embarrassed will follow you into the next course.

title: Teaching Philosophy
text:
The limits
We cannot meet the needs of every student, and we cannot make every student care. I have stopped treating that as a personal failure. But it does not change the math on the ones we can reach, and there are more of those than most people assume.
We can make a difference. That is enough reason to keep doing it carefully.

title: Lab 7: Impulse and Momentum
text:
At a glance

Questions. Two parts. Part 1: how does the change in a cart’s velocity depend on the impulse the wall gives it, and does it keep its kinetic energy through the bounce? Part 2: how does the momentum change of one cart compare with the momentum change of the other when they bounce, stick or fly apart, and what happens to the kinetic energy in each case?
You measure. Part 1: the cart’s velocity before and after it hits the wall and the impulse from the force sensor, ten runs at different speeds, plus the cart’s mass on the balance. Part 2: the velocity of cart A before the interaction and the velocities of both carts after it, nine runs (three kinds of interaction, three ways of placing the mass bar), plus the masses of both carts and the bar.
You calculate. Part 1: \(\Delta v\) and the kinetic energy before and after. Part 2: \(\Delta p\) and \(\Delta K\) for each cart. You type the formulas for \(\Delta v\) and both \(\Delta p\) columns yourself. The sheet builds \(M_A\) and \(M_B\) for every row from the three masses typed in above the Part 2 table.
You graph. Four graphs. Part 1: \(\Delta v\) against impulse, slope \(1/M\), and \(K_F\) against \(K_I\), slope compared with 1. Part 2: \(\Delta p_B\) against \(\Delta p_A\) for all nine runs, slope compared with \(-1\), and \(\Delta K_B\) against \(\Delta K_A\) for the three bouncy runs only, slope compared with \(-1\).
You conclude. Two paragraphs. Momentum first, both parts, with the cart mass and its percent difference from the balance. Kinetic energy second, both parts, with the wall bounce classified.

Three calculations on the Part 1 board and four on the Part 2 board, which is what the report template counts.
Some things about this sheet that are not obvious from looking at it:

What you type. The \(\Delta v\) column in Part 1 and the \(\Delta p_A\) and \(\Delta p_B\) columns in Part 2 are empty in the template. Enter those formulas yourself in the first row, then fill down. \(M_\text{CART}\) goes in the cell at the top of Part 1 and the three Part 2 masses in the row above its table, and every \(M_A\) and \(M_B\) is built from those.
Signs. Positive is the direction the cart was pushed. In Part 1 the cart comes back, so \(v_f\), \(J\) and \(\Delta v\) are all negative, and the sheet says so under the table. In Part 2, \(v_{i,A}\) is positive (zero in the explodey rows), \(\Delta p_A\) is negative, \(\Delta p_B\) is positive, and \(v_{f,A}\) can go either way. The mean row already handles the signs, so \(\delta_r = \delta_a / \text{mean}\) works as it always does.
What is filled in. Part 1 gives \(\delta_a = 0.01\ \text{m/s}\) for the velocities, \(0.001\ \text{N·s}\) for the impulse and \(0.001\ \text{kg}\) for the mass. Part 2 fills in the mass \(\delta_a\) and leaves the velocity cells blank. Use the same \(0.01\ \text{m/s}\), it is the same instrument.
The two uncertainty rows. \(\Delta v\) is a difference, so its \(\delta_a\) is the larger of the two velocity values, \(0.01\ \text{m/s}\), which is what the green cell is waiting for. The \(\Delta p\) columns are products, so their \(\delta_r\) is the largest \(\delta_r\) among their inputs, and the sheet colours them for you: the green inputs (\(M_A\), \(v_{i,A}\), \(v_{f,A}\)) feed the green \(\Delta p_A\), the blue inputs (\(M_B\), \(v_{f,B}\)) feed the blue \(\Delta p_B\), then \(\delta_a = \delta_r \times \text{mean}\). The uncertainty guide walks through both rules.
Kinetic energy. In Part 1 the \(K_I\) and \(K_F\) columns have their own mean, \(\delta_a\) and \(\delta_r\) cells, labelled in column N, with nothing filled in. Average them yourself, then the product rule. Part 2’s kinetic energy columns have no uncertainty rows. The template holds the kinetic energy formulas in first rows only: the first row of Part 1 for \(K_I\) and \(K_F\), the first row of each kind of run for \(K_{I,A}\) and \(K_{F,A}\), and the very first row for \(K_{F,B}\). Fill them all down before anything is graphed, or the \(\Delta K\) columns, which are already filled in, show zeros.
Decimal places. A kinetic energy here is a few hundredths of a joule, so the cells show 0.02 or 0.00 until decimals are added, and the sheet warns about this at the top. Add places until three significant figures show.

The graphs. Four of them, axes labelled with units on all four.

Part 1, \(\Delta v\) in m/s on the vertical axis against \(J\) in N·s on the horizontal, one linear trendline with its equation. The slope is \(1/M_\text{CART}\), in units of one over kilograms, so \(M_\text{EXP} = 1/\text{slope}\). If you plotted it the other way round, impulse vertical, the slope is the mass itself.
Part 1, \(K_F\) against \(K_I\), both in joules, one linear trendline. The slope has no units and is compared with 1.00, and \(1 - \text{slope}\) is the fraction of the kinetic energy that the bounce cost.
Part 2, \(\Delta p_B\) against \(\Delta p_A\), both in kg·m/s, all nine runs in one series, one linear trendline. The slope is compared with \(-1.00\).
Part 2, \(\Delta K_B\) against \(\Delta K_A\) in joules for the three bouncy rows only. The template has this chart drawn already and keeps the sticky and explodey \(\Delta K_B\) values in a separate column so they stay out of it. Add the linear trendline. Its slope is compared with \(-1\).



On the board
Left half, derivation. For Part 1, start from Newton’s second law in the form it was first written: force is the rate at which momentum changes, \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\). Multiply the time back in and add up the collision:
\[J = \int F\,dt = \Delta p = M\,\Delta v \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta v = \frac{1}{M}\,J.\]
A line through the origin with slope \(1/M\), which is why the slope of the first graph gives the cart’s mass. Then \(K = \tfrac12 M v^2\), so \(K_F / K_I = (v_f / v_i)^2\), and the second graph has slope 1 only if the cart leaves the wall as fast as it arrived.
For Part 2, use Newton’s third law. While the carts interact, the force of A on B and the force of B on A are equal and opposite at every instant, and they last for the same time, so the two impulses are equal and opposite:
\[\Delta p_B = -\,\Delta p_A, \qquad M_A v_{i,A} = M_A v_{f,A} + M_B v_{f,B}.\]
That is a line of slope \(-1\) through the origin on the third graph, and the second form is momentum conservation written out. Kinetic energy has no such law: \(\Delta K_A + \Delta K_B\) can be zero, negative or positive, and the three kinds of run exist to show all three.
Right half, sample calculations. Three for Part 1 and four for Part 2, each from one real row, every factor with its unit. Invented numbers, with \(M_\text{CART} = 0.261\ \text{kg}\), \(v_i = 0.420\ \text{m/s}\) and \(v_f = -0.378\ \text{m/s}\):
\[\Delta v = -0.378\ \text{m/s} - 0.420\ \text{m/s} = -0.798\ \text{m/s},\]
\[K_I = \tfrac12 (0.261\ \text{kg})(0.420\ \text{m/s})^2 = 0.0230\ \text{J}, \qquad K_F = \tfrac12 (0.261\ \text{kg})(0.378\ \text{m/s})^2 = 0.0186\ \text{J}, \qquad \Delta K = -0.0044\ \text{J},\]
\[M_\text{EXP} = \frac{1}{\text{slope}} = \frac{1}{3.76\ \text{kg}^{-1}} = 0.266\ \text{kg}.\]
For Part 2, take a bouncy row with the bar on B: \(M_A = 0.257\ \text{kg}\), \(M_B = 0.513\ \text{kg}\), \(v_{i,A} = 0.502\ \text{m/s}\), \(v_{f,A} = -0.158\ \text{m/s}\), \(v_{f,B} = 0.325\ \text{m/s}\):

text:
Common slips

Reporting the slope of \(\Delta v\) against \(J\) as the mass. The slope is \(1/M\), in one over kilograms. One divided by it is the mass.
A positive \(v_f\). The cart comes back the way it came, so \(v_f\), \(J\) and \(\Delta v\) are all negative. If \(J\) comes out positive while \(\Delta v\) is negative, the sensor’s sign is reversed, and the slope and the mass come out negative with it.
Reading \(v_i\) and \(v_f\) far from the collision. Friction slows the cart on the way in and on the way out, so take the flat stretches right next to the collision, and integrate the force across the collision only, because baseline noise adds up over a long selection.

The bar on the wrong cart for the row. The sheet builds \(M_A\) and \(M_B\) in a fixed order within each kind of run, bar on B, bar on A, no bar. Run the trials in that order or move the formulas.

Treating CON as someone else’s job. This week it is everyone’s.

title: Lab 7: Impulse and Momentum
text:
Going deeper
Impulse and momentum are the same unit. A newton is a kilogram metre per second squared, so a newton second is a kilogram metre per second, which is a momentum. The impulse the wall delivers is the momentum it takes from the cart, which is why one column is in N·s and the next is in m/s and the slope between them is in one over kilograms. Read that slope as a price: how much velocity one newton second buys. A heavy cart buys less. That is what mass means.
Why the slope is minus one. Newton’s third law says the two carts push on each other with equal and opposite forces at every instant. They also push for exactly the same time, because the interaction starts and stops for both at once. Equal force for equal time is equal and opposite impulse, so \(\Delta p_B = -\Delta p_A\) whatever the carts are made of and whatever their ends do. Momentum conservation is the third law with the time multiplied in. Nothing in that argument mentions kinetic energy, which is why the bouncy, sticky and explodey runs all land on the same line of slope \(-1\) and still do three different things to \(K\).
What the three mass arrangements show. For a bouncy collision with B at rest, \(v_{f,A} = \dfrac{M_A - M_B}{M_A + M_B}\,v_{i,A}\) and \(v_{f,B} = \dfrac{2M_A}{M_A + M_B}\,v_{i,A}\). Light A on heavy B: A bounces back. Heavy A on light B: A keeps going, slower. Equal masses: A stops dead and B leaves with A’s speed, which is Newton’s cradle in one click. So the \(v_{f,A}\) column should change sign between the first two bouncy rows and sit near zero in the third. In an explodey run the two carts leave with equal and opposite momentum, and since \(K = p^2 / 2M\) the lighter cart carries more of the energy, with the same \(p\) and a smaller \(M\) under it. In a sticky run the fraction of kinetic energy lost is \(M_B / (M_A + M_B)\), so the heavier the cart at rest, the more is lost.
Where the wall fits. Part 1 is Part 2 with a cart B of enormous mass. The cart’s momentum is not conserved on its own, because the wall, and the Earth it is bolted to, takes the difference. Put \(0.2\ \text{kg·m/s}\) into \(6 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\) and the Earth’s share of the velocity change is about \(3 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{m/s}\), which no instrument will ever see. Push \(M_B\) to infinity in the sticky fraction above and the loss goes to 100%, so a cart that stuck to the wall would stop dead and keep none of its energy. The wall bounce in Part 1 lives somewhere between that and a perfect rebound, and the slope of \(K_F\) against \(K_I\) says where.

Common slips

Using \(F_N = M_\text{TOT}\,g\) from Lab 4. On a slope the normal force is \(M_\text{TOT}\,g\cos\theta\), and the whole point of the lab is that the cosine is there.
Degrees where Excel wanted radians, which shows up as negative or absurd normal forces.
Recording the angle the track was set to rather than the angle at which the block moved.
Fitting the velocity–time graph over a stretch that includes the moment of release or the stop at the bottom. Fit only the straight, sliding part.

title: Lab 5: Friction on an Incline
text:
Going deeper
The angle alone gives the static coefficient. Divide the slipping condition by the normal force: \(\mu_s = f_{s,\max}/F_N = \sin\theta/\cos\theta = \tan\theta_\text{MAX}\). The mass cancels. So every row of your table, whatever the load, should slip at about the same angle, and a block that slips at 20.5° has \(\mu_s = \tan 20.5^\circ = 0.37\) before you have graphed anything. If your slipping angles drift upward as the load grows, something other than friction is going on, and that is worth a sentence in the conclusion.
Why we still make the graph. One angle gives one number. Five loads on a graph give a slope, an intercept that should be near zero, and a visible check that the points fall on a line at all. The graph is how you find out whether \(f = \mu F_N\) was the right model, not just what \(\mu\) is.
Same coefficients as Lab 4? For the same two surfaces they should be, within uncertainty. Nothing in the question asks for the comparison, but if your numbers from Lab 4 are handy, a percent difference between the two weeks is a good test of both.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text: Every lab I teach, no matter how many times I have explained it, I get questions about uncertainty. That is not a complaint. Uncertainty is confusing the first few times you meet it, and a lab period is a bad place to learn it. This page is the answer I would give you if we had the time: the quick version first, for the lab you are doing right now, and the longer story after it for anyone who wants to know why. If you find it confusing, you are in good company.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text:
Uncertainty or Error?






TipThe short version



Error is how far off you were. Uncertainty is how well you know the number. The first needs a right answer to compare against. The second does not.


In daily life the two words are close to interchangeable. In a physics lab they are not, and most of the confusion on this page comes from letting them blur together, so let me pull them apart on purpose.
Start with “oops.” You say it when you made a mistake: you dropped something, you added where you should have subtracted, you read the wrong row of the table. That is the everyday meaning of error, and it is worth holding onto, because the lab meaning is its well-behaved cousin. In a lab report, error is how far your result landed from the value you expected. If I know my coffee is \(180^\circ\mathrm{F}\) and my thermometer reads \(175^\circ\mathrm{F}\), the error is \(5^\circ\mathrm{F}\). When a lab asks for a percent error, this is the number it wants: the gap between your answer and the accepted one, as a fraction of the accepted one.
Nobody has ever said “oops, I made an uncertainty.” Uncertainty is what you say with “I’m not sure.” Ask me how hot my coffee is when I have no thermometer and I can still answer, but only from what I know: boiling water is \(212^\circ\mathrm{F}\), the cup has been sitting for a minute, it is still too hot to drink. So, “about \(190^\circ\mathrm{F}\), give or take \(20\).” The give-or-take is the uncertainty. It is not a mistake. It is an honest statement of how well I know the number, and the honest version of my answer is “somewhere between \(170\) and \(210^\circ\mathrm{F}\), probably.”
So the two words answer two different questions. Error asks how far off was I? and needs a right answer to compare against. Uncertainty asks how well do I know this? and needs no right answer at all. You can put an uncertainty on a measurement nobody has ever made before. That is the whole distinction.
One warning: physicists have been sloppy about this for a century. You will see “error bars” on graphs that are really uncertainty bars, and the Lab Professor’s primer calls the whole subject error analysis. When you read “error” in a textbook, check which question it is answering. On this page, and in my grading, error is the gap and uncertainty is the give-or-take.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text:
Why Does Uncertainty Matter?
Say we are meeting for dinner and I tell you I will be there at 7. Neither of us thinks I mean 7:00:00.000. I mean around 7, give or take a bit, and the size of that bit is the uncertainty on my arrival time. If it is a few minutes, nobody cares. If it is two hours, you care a great deal, because “7 PM plus or minus 2 hours” means anywhere from 5 to 9, and you are either sitting alone at a table for hours or checking the door every five minutes. The number 7 never changed. What changed is how much the number is worth.
That is the job uncertainty does in science. A measurement with no uncertainty is “7 PM” with no way to tell whether it means 7 sharp or “sometime this evening.” The second number tells the reader how hard they are allowed to lean on the first. A number you cannot lean on is not a result.






NoteUncertainty as confidence



There is one more layer, and it is the one that makes the \(\pm\) precise instead of vague. “7 PM \(\pm\) 2 hours” does not mean I am guaranteed to arrive between 5 and 9. It means I am fairly confident I will. When the uncertainty is a proper statistical one (a standard deviation from repeated measurements, which the Lab Professor’s primer walks through), “fairly confident” has a number attached: about a \(68\%\) chance I arrive within one uncertainty of 7, so between 5 and 9; about \(95\%\) within two, between 3 and 11; and \(99.7\%\) within three, between 1 PM and 1 AM.
Notice what the \(68\%\) means for you. There is roughly a one-in-three chance I show up outside 5 to 9. When are you even supposed to leave the house? Widen the window and I get more confident, but the window gets less useful: “I will almost certainly arrive between 1 PM and 1 AM” is both true and worthless. Every measurement lives in that tension. The honest window and the useful window pull in opposite directions, and the quality of an experiment is how narrow a window it can honestly claim.
The uncertainties you estimate in this lab, like half a millimeter on a meter stick, are judgments rather than standard deviations from repeated trials, so do not read the \(68\%\) off them too literally. The idea is the same: the \(\pm\) is a statement of confidence, not a fence.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text:
Measurement Uncertainty
There are two kinds of uncertainty in these labs, and the quick guide above sorts every column into one or the other. The first is measurement uncertainty: the uncertainty you get for no other reason than that no instrument reads infinitely finely.
Measure your desk with a ruler marked only in inches. The best you can do is “about 16 inches,” or if you are careful, “about halfway between 16 and 17.” Either way the inch marks set the limit. You can estimate between them, and that estimate is where your judgment comes in, but you cannot get a hundredth of an inch out of a ruler that only shows inches.
Swap in a ruler marked in millimeters and the same desk comes out as “405 mm,” or “405.3 mm” if you trust yourself to read between the lines. Better instrument, smaller uncertainty, never zero. Nobody with a meter stick can tell me their desk is \(405.728467\) mm long, and a number written that way is not more precise. It is a claim the instrument cannot back up. The instrument sets the floor, and your honesty decides how close to it you get.
This is why the quick guide asks what you measured with before it asks anything else. The uncertainty on a measured column is not a formula. It is a judgment about the tool: the finest division you could actually read, or the size of the wobble if the reading would not sit still. I grade that judgment on whether it is reasonable, not on whether it matches a number in my head.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text:
Calculated Uncertainty
The second kind shows up the moment you use a measurement. Suppose I measure the desk as \(405 \pm 1\) mm on each side and want its area. Whatever the area comes out to, I cannot know it better than I knew the sides. The uncertainty in the lengths has to flow through the multiplication into the area. That is calculated uncertainty, and the two rules in the quick guide are the two ways it flows.
Adding and subtracting pass along the biggest absolute uncertainty. Picture the total mass in the friction lab: a box whose mass was handed to you as \(0.11\) kg, with a bar on top known to \(\pm 10\) g. The total is uncertain by about \(10\) g, because the bar’s fuzziness is the only fuzziness there is, and nothing about the box can shrink it. So a sum carries the largest \(\delta_a\) of its pieces.
Multiplying and dividing pass along the biggest relative uncertainty. Here the honest comparison is percentages, not amounts. Take the Lab Professor’s example: two lengths, \(20.35 \pm 0.05\) m and \(7.61 \pm 0.02\) m. The first has the bigger absolute uncertainty, but as a fraction of itself it is only \(0.2\%\), while the second is \(0.3\%\). Multiply them for an area and it is the \(0.3\%\) that limits the answer, because a \(0.3\%\) fuzz in one factor is a \(0.3\%\) fuzz in the product, however large the product gets. So a product carries the largest \(\delta_r\) of its factors, and you convert back to an amount at the end by multiplying by the product itself: \(0.0026 \times 154.86\ \mathrm{m^2} \approx 0.4\ \mathrm{m^2}\).
Why percentages for products and amounts for sums? Because of what each operation does to a small nudge. Nudge one term of a sum by \(0.05\) and the sum moves by exactly \(0.05\): amounts pass straight through addition. Nudge one factor of a product by \(0.3\%\) and the product moves by \(0.3\%\): fractions pass straight through multiplication. The two rules are one rule, “the result inherits the nudge,” written in whichever currency the operation deals in.






NoteThe honest version



“Take the biggest one” is a deliberate simplification, and it is the rule this lab uses, so use it. The full treatment, which is in the Lab Professor’s primer and in any statistics course, combines uncertainties in quadrature: for a sum, \(\delta_a^2 = \delta_{a,1}^2 + \delta_{a,2}^2\), and the same shape for relative uncertainties in a product. A root of a sum of squares always lands between “the biggest one” and “all of them added up,” so the biggest one is a fair stand-in whenever one input dominates, which in these labs it nearly always does. For anyone who has had calculus, the general rule is \(\delta_A^2 = \sum_i \left(\partial A/\partial X_i\right)^2 \delta_{X_i}^2\), and the lab rules are what it collapses to when one term wins.

title: Measurement Uncertainty
text:
Writing It Down
A measurement is not finished until it is written as value \(\pm\) uncertainty, with units on both, and the two numbers have to agree about how many digits are real. The convention in these labs: round the uncertainty to one significant figure, then round the value to the same decimal place. The area above came out of the calculator as \(154.8635\ \mathrm{m^2}\) with \(\delta_a = 0.407\ \mathrm{m^2}\). Written honestly, it is \(154.9 \pm 0.4\ \mathrm{m^2}\). Every digit past the tenths place was fiction, and the uncertainty is what told you so.
This is also where error and uncertainty finally meet. When a lab asks you to compare your result with an accepted value, you now hold both numbers: how far off you were, and how far off you were allowed to be. If the accepted value sits inside your \(\pm\) window, your measurement agrees with it, full stop, even if the percent error is not zero. If it sits outside, something systematic happened, and working out what is the most interesting paragraph you can write in a conclusion. That is the whole point of the second number.

The second is the one I care about more. I like taking high-level physics and breaking it down to a level where anyone can actually engage with it — not a watered-down version, the real thing explained properly. Most people who think they are bad at physics have only ever met explanations written for people who already understood. The Teaching section is my attempt at the other kind, and it is free, permanently, to anyone who wants it.

title: Teaching Resources
text:
Most of the time, when a student tells me they are bad at physics, what they actually mean is that nobody has ever explained it to them in a language they already speak. That is a translation problem, not an ability problem, and it is fixable.
So this section exists to be the explanation I wish someone had handed me: slower where it matters, honest about what is genuinely hard, and never pretending a step is obvious when it isn’t.

title: Teaching Resources
text:
How these are written
I try to hold to a few rules across everything in this section.
Start below the starting point. If a lesson needs an idea from three courses ago, the lesson explains that idea rather than assuming it. The Python series opens with information theory for exactly this reason.
Name the hard part out loud. Some things are genuinely difficult. Saying “as you can clearly see” about a step that took me an hour is a disservice, and it teaches students that their confusion is a personal failing.
Give you something to poke at. Reading about a for loop does very little. Running one, breaking it, and running it again does quite a lot. Code on this site is live wherever it can be.
Keep the physics attached to something real. Every abstraction started as someone trying to answer a concrete question. That question is usually the best way in.
There is more on where this comes from in my teaching philosophy.

title: How a Lab Gets Turned In
text:
Every lab in this course is turned in the same way. Your group splits into three jobs, each job fills one whiteboard, and photos of the boards go into the Word template alongside your screenshots. The jobs are QPD (Question, Procedure, Diagram), UDA (Uncertainty, Data, Analysis) and CON (Conclusion). After “what uncertainty do I put here?”, the question I get most is “does this look okay?”, so this page is the answer: what belongs on each board, where it sits, and a checklist to run before anyone takes a photo.
The boards are about 75 cm by 50 cm. That is not much room, so what goes on one has to be chosen, and the layouts below are the ones that fit.

NoteRegular labs and major labs




Regular labs. You turn in the part you worked on. In a group of two, one person does QPD, the other does UDA, both write CON, and each of you turns in your own part plus CON.

Before you take the photo
Run this on every board, whatever the job. It takes thirty seconds and catches most of what I take points off for.


Your name and your job label (QPD, UDA or CON) are in the header at the top.
Every number has a unit, including the ones inside equations and on axes.

title: How a Lab Gets Turned In
text:
The QPD board
The test of a QPD board is simple: someone who has never seen the equipment should be able to read it, repeat your experiment, and know exactly which numbers you wrote down and in what units.

  QPDYour name · partners' names
  Q: What is the relationship between $x$ and $y$? (the real quantities, in words)
  
    Procedure
    
      Numbered steps, in the order you did them.
      Every measured quantity named with its symbol and unit the first time it appears.
      What you held fixed, what you varied, how many trials.
      Where each number was read from (the Statistics box, the angle scale, the fit).
    
    Diagram: an annotated photo in Word, or drawn here or on a second board
  

The QPD board. The header and the question take two lines; the procedure gets everything else.

Header. Job label on the left, names on the right, a line under both.
The question, written as a title under the header. It always has the form “What is the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\)?”, and \(x\) and \(y\) are the physical quantities in words: “the normal force on the block and the friction force between the block and the track”, not “\(F_N\) and \(f\)”. If the lab has more than one surface, spring or object, name them. The symbols can follow in brackets.
The procedure, filling the rest of the board. Numbered steps in the order you did them, written for a reader who knows nothing about the lab. Name every quantity you measured, with its symbol and its unit, and say where the number came from: “read the maximum static friction force \(f_{s,\max}\) in newtons from the Statistics box over the peak.” Say what you held fixed and what you varied.
The diagram. Most groups take a photo of the setup and annotate it in Word with arrows and labels on every measurable quantity: positions, distances, angles, which surface is which. Drawing it instead is fine, on a split board or a second one. Either way, “annotated” means labels. A photo with no labels is a photo, not a diagram.



The question starts “What is the relationship between” and names real quantities, not letters.
Each measured quantity appears in the procedure with a symbol and a unit.
The procedure says how many trials and which values you stepped through.
A stranger could tell from the steps where each number in the data table came from.
The diagram or photo has labels on every quantity that was measured.

title: How a Lab Gets Turned In
text:
The UDA board
The UDA job is two jobs. Most of it happens in Excel and never touches the board; the board is where you show the physics behind the spreadsheet.
In Excel, not on the board:

Data in the yellow cells, every calculated column completed, and both uncertainty rows for every column. The uncertainty guide walks through those two rows column by column.
The graph: the right quantities on the right axes, axis labels with units, one series per data set, a linear trendline on each series with its equation showing, and a legend that says which series is which.
Nearly every lab ends in a straight line, even when the relationship being tested is not linear, because we choose what to plot so that the line comes out straight and its slope means something. That graph is the linearized graph, and its trendline equation is the one the conclusion quotes.

On the board:

  UDAYour name · partners' names
  
    
      FBD + derivation
      The free-body diagram, with every force labelled.
      The force equations that follow from it.
      The relationship you are about to graph, in the lab's own symbols.
    
    
      Sample calculations
      One per calculated column, from a real row:
      $M_\text{tot} = 0.25\,\text{kg} + 0.11\,\text{kg} = 0.36\,\text{kg}$
      $F_N = (0.36\,\text{kg})(9.81\,\text{m/s}^2) = 3.5\,\text{N}$
      … and so on down the calculated columns
    
  

The UDA board. Left half: where the formulas come from. Right half: proof that the spreadsheet uses them.

Header, as before.
Left half: the derivation. Whatever gets from the physics to the quantity on the graph. Often that is a free-body diagram, the force equations it implies, and the relationship that falls out; sometimes it is shorter. Label every force on the diagram and define every symbol.
Right half: one sample calculation for every calculated column in the sheet. Pick a real row, write the measured numbers that feed it with their units, and show the arithmetic. One or two lines per column is enough. This is what proves the formula in the spreadsheet is the one from the physics, and it is where missing units get noticed, so put them in.



Every force on the free-body diagram is labelled and every symbol is defined.
The derivation ends with the relationship that the graph tests.
There is one sample calculation for every calculated column, with numbers from a real row.
Every number in the sample calculations carries a unit, and the result has the column’s unit.
In Excel: both uncertainty rows are filled for every column, the axes are labelled with units, and each trendline’s equation is on the chart with a legend naming the series.

title: How a Lab Gets Turned In
text:
The CON board
One paragraph. The instructions for the conclusion arrive as a numbered list of four or five questions, and each question becomes exactly one sentence, in order. No bullet points, no headings, no “Q1:”. Someone reading only your paragraph should come away knowing what you found, how big it was, and how it compares with what was expected.

  CONYour name · partners' names
  
    1 The relationship between $x$ and $y$ is linear / quadratic / ….
    2 The trendline equation(s), in the lab's symbols with units.
    3 The result(s), with units and what they describe.
    4 Sometimes: a comparison inside your own results.
    5 The comparison to a reference value, as a percent difference.
    one paragraph, one sentence per question, in order
  

The CON board. The numbers are here to show the order; they do not go on the board.
The sentences, one by one. Examples use the friction lab, with invented numbers.

The answer to the lab question, in the words of the QPD question. “The relationship between the normal force on the block and the friction force on it is linear, for both static and kinetic friction.”
The trendline equation, rewritten in the lab’s symbols with units. Excel gives you \(y = 0.314x + 0.02\). You write \(f_s = (0.314)\,F_N + 0.02\ \text{N}\), and you say that the coefficient is unitless because it is a force divided by a force. One equation per data set. If the relationship graph and the linearized graph are different graphs, quote both equations.
The result, with units and with what it describes: “The coefficient of static friction between cork and poplar is 0.31.” All of them, if there are several.
Sometimes, a comparison inside your results, when a question asks for it: “The static coefficient was larger than the kinetic coefficient for both surfaces.”
The comparison to a reference: a known value, another measurement, or the class mean, usually as a percent difference. Use the formula the week’s instructions give; the two in circulation are \(\%\,\text{error} = 100\%\,(M - T)/T\) against a true value \(T\) and \(\%\,\text{difference} = 200\%\,(M_1 - M_2)/(M_1 + M_2)\) between two measurements.



It is a paragraph: one sentence per question, in the order the questions were asked.
Sentence one repeats the QPD question’s quantities and names the kind of relationship.
Every equation uses the lab’s symbols, not \(x\) and \(y\), with units on every term that has them.
Every result has a unit, or a sentence saying why it has none.
The comparison names what it compares against and gives a percentage.

title: Lab 4: Friction on a Flat Surface

At a glance

Question. How does the friction force on a block depend on the normal force pressing it into the track, for static and for kinetic friction, on two different pairs of surfaces?
You measure. The peak force just before the block slips and the average force while it slides, for five loads, three trials each, on two surface combinations.
You calculate. The total mass on the track and the normal force.
You graph. Friction force against normal force: four data sets on one graph, four linear trendlines. The four slopes are the four coefficients of friction.
You conclude. The relationship in words, the four equations, the four coefficients, static against kinetic, surface against surface.

title: Lab 4: Friction on a Flat Surface
text:
CON
The questions as they are handed out, each with the sentence it becomes. The numbers are invented.

What relationship did you find between the normal force and the friction force, both static and kinetic? → “The relationship between the normal force on the block and the friction force on it is linear, for both static and kinetic friction and for both surface combinations.”
What were your two static-friction trendlines and your two kinetic-friction trendlines? Physical variables, not \(x\) and \(y\). → “For cork on oak the trendlines were \(f_s = (0.31)\,F_N\) and \(f_k = (0.24)\,F_N\), and for felt on oak they were \(f_s = (0.42)\,F_N\) and \(f_k = (0.35)\,F_N\).” If Excel gives an intercept, keep it, with its unit: \(+\,0.05\ \text{N}\).
What were your four friction coefficients? → “The coefficients were \(\mu_s = 0.31\) and \(\mu_k = 0.24\) for cork on oak and \(\mu_s = 0.42\) and \(\mu_k = 0.35\) for felt on oak, to two significant figures; they are unitless because each is a force divided by a force.”
Were the kinetic or the static coefficients greater in general? → “For both combinations the static coefficient was larger than the kinetic one.”
Which surface combination had the larger coefficients? → “Felt on oak had the larger coefficients for both static and kinetic friction.”

There is no outside reference value in this lab. The comparison is between your own results.

title: Lab 4: Friction on a Flat Surface
text:
Common slips

Writing \(y = 0.314x + 0.02\) instead of \(f_s = (0.314)\,F_N + 0.02\ \text{N}\).
Four trendlines and no legend, so nobody can tell which is which.
Leaving the box out of the total mass.
Reading \(f_k\) off the peak, or \(f_{s,\max}\) off the plateau.
Pulling at an angle or in jerks. The sensor measures tension, and tension only equals friction when the pull is horizontal and the block is not accelerating.
Coefficients quoted to five figures. Two is what is asked for, and two is what the data support.
crumbs: Lab 4: Friction on a Flat Surface

title: Lab 4: Friction on a Flat Surface
text:
Going deeper
Why the coefficient has no units. It is the ratio of two forces, so the newtons cancel. That also tells you what it measures: how many newtons of sideways push each newton of squeeze can resist before the surfaces let go.
Why static beats kinetic. When the block sits still, the high points of the two surfaces settle into each other and tiny bonds form. Breaking them takes more force than keeping them broken; once the block is sliding, it rides over the high points before new contacts can fully form. So \(\mu_s \ge \mu_k\), and your fourth sentence is checking exactly that.
Why the contact area never appears. Guillaume Amontons wrote this down in 1699, two centuries after Leonardo da Vinci sketched it: friction depends on the load and not on the apparent area of contact. The real contact area, the tips of the bumps that actually touch, is a tiny fraction of the apparent one, and it grows in proportion to the load. Double the squeeze, double the real contact, double the friction. Area drops out.

title: Lab 6: The Spring Constant, Two Ways
text:
At a glance

Questions. Two of them. Part 1: how does the force a spring exerts depend on how far it is stretched? Part 2: how does the farthest stretch of a dropped mass depend on the mass?
You measure. Part 1: a hanging mass and the spring’s position before and after it is lowered gently to rest, seven masses. Part 2: the position before release and the lowest point reached, three drops per mass.
You calculate. The stretch \(\Delta y\) in meters for both parts, the spring force in newtons for Part 1, and the spring constant from each graph’s slope.
You graph. Part 1: spring force against stretch. Part 2: maximum stretch against mass. Both linear.
You conclude. Both relationships in words, both equations, both spring constants, and the percent difference between them.

On the board
Left half, derivation. For Part 1, draw the hanging mass at rest with two forces, the spring force up and the weight down. At rest they balance: \(F_\text{spring} = Mg\). That is why a column of masses becomes a column of forces, and Hooke’s law \(F_\text{spring} = k\,\Delta y\) says the graph should be a line through the origin with slope \(k\).
For Part 2 the mass is not at rest, so forces alone will not do it; use energy. Released from the unstretched position, the mass falls \(\Delta y\) and stops for an instant at the bottom. The gravitational energy it gave up, \(Mg\,\Delta y\), is all in the spring, \(\tfrac12 k\,\Delta y^2\). Set them equal and cancel one \(\Delta y\):
\[Mg\,\Delta y = \tfrac12 k\,\Delta y^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta y = \frac{2g}{k}\,M.\]
A line through the origin with slope \(2g/k\). If your instructor has you plot \(M\) against \(\Delta y\) instead, the slope is \(k/2g\) and \(k = 2g \times \text{slope}\).
Right half, three sample calculations, as the template asks: one \(\Delta y\), one \(F_\text{spring}\), and the spring constant from the second graph’s slope. Invented numbers:
\[\Delta y = \frac{34.6\ \text{cm} - 22.1\ \text{cm}}{100} = 0.125\ \text{m}, \qquad F_\text{spring} = \frac{250\ \text{g}}{1000}\,(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2) = 2.45\ \text{N},\]
\[k = \frac{2g}{\text{slope}} = \frac{2\,(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)}{0.98\ \text{m/kg}} = 20\ \text{N/m}.\]

title: Lab 6: The Spring Constant, Two Ways
text:
Common slips

Mass where a force belongs. The vertical axis of the first graph is \(Mg\) in newtons, not \(M\) in grams, and the slope is only a spring constant if it is.
Grams and centimeters leaking into the answer. The sheet divides by 1000 and by 100 for a reason; the sample calculation on the board must show the same conversions.
A spring constant with no units, or in N/cm. It is N/m.
Giving the mass a push on release, or catching the lowest point late. Both make \(\Delta y\) too large and \(k_2\) too small.
Mixing up which slope needs the \(2g\). The force-against-stretch slope is \(k\). The stretch-against-mass slope is \(2g/k\).

title: Lab 6: The Spring Constant, Two Ways
text:
Going deeper
Why dropping stretches the spring twice as far. Hang the mass gently and it settles where \(k\,\Delta y_1 = Mg\), so \(\Delta y_1 = Mg/k\). Drop it and the energy argument gives \(\Delta y_2 = 2Mg/k\). Exactly double. At the resting point the spring force only just matches the weight, but the falling mass arrives there with speed, overshoots, and keeps stretching until the spring has absorbed all the energy it brought, which takes twice the distance. If you ever wondered why a climber’s rope has to be rated for far more than the climber’s weight, this is the start of the answer.
Where the factor of one half comes from. The spring force grows from zero to \(k\,\Delta y\) as the spring stretches, so the work it does is the average force, \(\tfrac12 k\,\Delta y\), times the distance \(\Delta y\). That is the area of a triangle under the force–stretch line, and it is the same triangle your Part 1 graph draws.
What “the same \(k\)” is testing. Part 1 uses forces in balance; Part 2 uses energy in motion. They should agree because they are two descriptions of one spring, and the percent difference in your last sentence is a measurement of how well two different pieces of physics line up on the same object.

At a glance

Questions. Two parts. Part 1: how does the force needed to balance a fixed torque depend on how far from the axle it acts? Part 2: how does the angular velocity of the rotor change with time when the torque on it is left unbalanced?
You measure. Part 1: the balancing force \(F_T\) at seven distances \(r_b\) from the axle, plus the hanging mass \(M_H\) and the radius of the pipe. Part 2: the clock time every time a mark on the rotor passes a reference line, half a turn apart, seventeen times.
You calculate. Part 1: \(1/r_b\), then the balancing torque \(\tau\) from a slope and the pipe radius \(r_a\) from \(\tau\). Part 2: \(\theta\), \(\Delta t\), \(\omega = \Delta\theta / \Delta t\) and \(t_\text{MID}\), then the angular acceleration \(\alpha\) two ways.
You graph. Four graphs. Part 1: \(F_T\) against \(r_b\) with a curved trendline, and \(F_T\) against \(1/r_b\) with a linear one whose slope is \(\tau\). Part 2: \(\omega\) against \(t_\text{MID}\), linear, slope \(\alpha\), and \(\theta\) against \(t\) with a second-order polynomial for the second value of \(\alpha\).
You conclude. One paragraph: both relationships, both equations, \(\tau\), \(r_a\) and \(\alpha\), the percent difference between \(r_a\) and the pipe’s measured radius, and the two values of \(\alpha\).

This lab has two parts, and the report template has a QPD slot for each: a board photo and an annotated setup photo for Part 1, and the same again for Part 2. Split one board or use two.
The templates do not name the apparatus, so this page calls whatever turns on the axle the rotor: the bar, disc or platform with the pipe at its centre.

The questions

Part 1: What is the relationship between the distance from the axle at which the balancing force acts (\(r_b\)) and the size of the balancing force (\(F_T\))?


Part 2: What is the relationship between the angular velocity of the rotor (\(\omega\)) and time (\(t\)) when the torque on it is unbalanced?

Part 2 also graphs the angle the rotor has turned through against time. If your instructor wants that as a question too, write it as a second line under the first: the relationship between the angle (\(\theta\)) and time (\(t\)).


What the procedure must make clear
The details below are the usual way a torque lab like this runs. Where the handout differs, the handout wins.

Part 1: what hangs from the string wound around the pipe, and its mass \(M_H\). That hanging mass makes the fixed torque that everything in Part 1 balances.

Part 1: how the pipe’s own radius was measured, for the comparison in CON. Calipers across the diameter, halved, is the usual way. The sheet has no cell for \(M_H\) or for the pipe radius, so both go in the procedure and on the board.

Two calculations on the Part 1 board and four on the Part 2 board, plus the second value of \(\alpha\), which is what the report template asks for.
Some things about this sheet that are not obvious from looking at it:

The colours. Yellow cells are typed in. Light green (Part 1) and light blue (Part 2) cells are formulas. Grey cells are not used. In Part 1 every green cell is empty, the mean and uncertainty rows included, so type the formula for \(1/r_b\) in the first row and fill it down, then =AVERAGE for each mean and \(\delta_a / \text{mean}\) for each \(\delta_r\). In Part 2 the colours stop at row 19 until you fill down.
Part 2 runs on two alternating rows. The clock times go in the yellow cells of every other row. A row with a time holds \(t\) and \(\theta\) at that moment. The row under it holds \(\Delta t\), \(\Delta\theta\), \(\omega\) and \(t_\text{MID}\) for the half turn that follows, which is why each \(\omega\) sits between two times. Only rows 17 to 19 have formulas. Select B18 to G19, both rows together, and drag the fill handle down to row 49, so Excel copies the two-row pattern. Dragging a single row breaks it. If it worked, the last \(\theta\) is \(16\pi = 50.27\ \text{rad}\).
\(\Delta\theta\) is the one yellow cell with a formula. It is =PI(), half a turn. If your marks were a full turn apart, change it to =2*PI() before you fill down, because every row below gets its own copy.
Radians. \(\theta\) in rad, \(\omega\) in rad/s, \(\alpha\) in rad/s². Not degrees, not revolutions.
Uncertainty, Part 1. \(r_b\) and \(F_T\) are measured, so their yellow \(\delta_a\) cells come from the instrument, as the uncertainty guide describes for measured columns. \(1/r_b\) is a power, so its \(\delta_r\) is the \(\delta_r\) of \(r_b\) and \(\delta_a = \delta_r \times \text{mean}\), the product rule.
Uncertainty, Part 2. The sheet gives \(\delta_a = 0.01\ \text{s}\) for \(t\) and \(\Delta t\). \(\theta\) and \(\Delta\theta\) are counted, not measured: each half turn adds exactly \(\pi\), and \(\pi\) is a constant, so both have \(\delta_a = 0\) and all of the timing uncertainty sits in \(t\) and \(\Delta t\). \(\omega\) is a quotient, so its \(\delta_r\) is the \(\delta_r\) of \(\Delta t\). \(t_\text{MID}\) adds two times and halves them, which is a mix, so its \(\delta_r\) is the \(\delta_r\) of \(t\). Only \(t\) and \(\theta\) have mean cells filled in. For the others, type =AVERAGE over the whole column, since it skips the blank rows.

The graphs. Four of them, axes labelled with units on all four.

Part 1, \(F_T\) in newtons on the vertical axis against \(r_b\) in meters on the horizontal, with a trendline and its equation. The template asks for two Part 1 graphs with their fits but does not name this one’s fit. A power trendline suits it, and an exponent close to \(-1\) means the force goes as one over the radius.
Part 1, \(F_T\) against \(1/r_b\) in 1/m, one linear trendline with its equation. The slope is the balancing torque \(\tau\) in N·m, since newtons divided by one over meters is newton meters. The intercept should be close to zero. If you plotted it the other way round, the slope is \(1/\tau\).
Part 2, \(\omega\) in rad/s against \(t_\text{MID}\) in seconds, one linear trendline. The slope is \(\alpha\) in rad/s². The intercept is the angular velocity at the first mark, which is not zero if the rotor was already turning when the timing started.
Part 2, \(\theta\) in radians against \(t\) in seconds, with a polynomial trendline of order 2. The coefficient of \(t^2\) is \(\alpha/2\), so \(\alpha = 2 \times\) that coefficient. The report template asks for one Part 2 graph, but the comparison on the board needs this one as well.



On the board
Left half, derivation. For Part 1, start from what a torque is. A force \(F\) pulling at right angles to a line of length \(r\) from the axle makes a torque \(\tau = rF\), which is why a door handle sits on the side away from the hinges. Two torques act on the still rotor. The string on the pipe pulls with the weight of the hanging mass, \(M_H g\), at radius \(r_a\), and turns it one way. \(F_T\) at radius \(r_b\) turns it the other way. Still means balanced:
\[F_T\,r_b = M_H g\,r_a = \tau \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F_T = \tau\,\frac{1}{r_b}.\]
Here \(\tau\) is the same for every run, because \(M_H\) and \(r_a\) never change. That makes \(F_T\) against \(r_b\) an inverse relationship, and \(F_T\) against \(1/r_b\) a line through the origin with slope \(\tau\). Then \(r_a = \tau / (M_H g)\). The report template writes the string’s tension as \(F_T = M_H g\). This page keeps \(F_T\) for the balancing force in the sheet’s column and writes the string’s tension as \(M_H g\), so the two do not get mixed up on the board.
For Part 2, nothing balances the hanging mass, so the net torque is constant but not zero, and a constant net torque gives a constant angular acceleration. With \(\alpha\) constant, the rotational versions of the constant-acceleration equations hold:
\[\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12 \alpha t^2, \qquad \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t.\]
Here \(\omega_0\) is the angular velocity at the first mark, \(t = 0\). The sheet never measures \(\omega\) at an instant. It measures how long each half turn took, so \(\Delta\theta / \Delta t\) is an average over the half turn. Which moment does that average belong to? Take two marks at \(t_1\) and \(t_2\):
\[\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} = \frac{\omega_0 (t_2 - t_1) + \tfrac12 \alpha \left(t_2^2 - t_1^2\right)}{t_2 - t_1} = \omega_0 + \alpha\,\frac{t_1 + t_2}{2} = \omega(t_\text{MID}).\]
The average over the half turn is exactly the angular velocity at the middle time. That is why the sheet pairs each \(\omega\) with \(t_\text{MID}\), and why \(\omega\) against \(t_\text{MID}\) is a line with slope \(\alpha\) while \(\theta\) against \(t\) is a parabola with \(t^2\) coefficient \(\alpha/2\).
Right half, sample calculations. For Part 1, one \(1/r_b\) and the pipe radius. Invented numbers, with \(M_H = 0.500\ \text{kg}\) and a slope of \(0.0804\ \text{N·m}\):
\[\frac{1}{r_b} = \frac{1}{0.125\ \text{m}} = 8.00\ \text{m}^{-1}, \qquad r_a = \frac{\tau}{M_H g} = \frac{0.0804\ \text{N·m}}{(0.500\ \text{kg})(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)} = 0.0164\ \text{m}.\]
For Part 2, one each of \(\theta\), \(\Delta t\), \(\omega\) and \(t_\text{MID}\): \(\theta\) at the fourth mark, then the other three for the half turn from the fourth mark to the fifth. The clock read 4.89 s and 5.38 s at those two marks, and 2.14 s at the first:
\[\theta = 6.28\ \text{rad} + 3.14\ \text{rad} = 9.42\ \text{rad}, \qquad \Delta t = 5.38\ \text{s} - 4.89\ \text{s} = 0.49\ \text{s},\]
\[\omega = \frac{3.14\ \text{rad}}{0.49\ \text{s}} = 6.41\ \text{rad/s}, \qquad t_\text{MID} = \frac{2.75\ \text{s} + 3.24\ \text{s}}{2} = 2.995\ \text{s}.\]
Then the two values of \(\alpha\), one from each graph:
\[\alpha_\omega = \text{slope} = 1.84\ \text{rad/s}^2, \qquad \alpha_\theta = 2\,(0.923\ \text{rad/s}^2) = 1.85\ \text{rad/s}^2.\]

The rotational acceleration was \(1.84\ \text{rad/s}^2\) from the slope of \(\omega\) against \(t_\text{MID}\) and \(1.85\ \text{rad/s}^2\) from the \(\theta\) against \(t\) graph, a percent difference of 0.5%.” The template asks only for the two values of \(\alpha\), so the percent difference between them is optional. If you give one, the primer’s percent difference between two measurements, \(200\%\,(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)/(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)\), fits it.

title: Lab 8: Balanced and Unbalanced Torque
text:
Common slips

Measuring \(r_b\) from the edge of the pipe or the end of the bar. The lever arm runs from the centre of the axle to the point where the force acts.
Pulling at an angle. Only the part of the force at right angles to the radius makes a torque, so a slanted pull reads high and its point sits above the line.
Reporting the slope as the radius. The slope of \(F_T\) against \(1/r_b\) is the torque, in N·m. Divide it by \(M_H g\) to get \(r_a\).
Losing \(M_H\) or the pipe’s measured radius. Neither has a cell in the sheet, and CON needs both. Write them down before the setup is taken apart.
Centimeters. An \(r_b\) in centimeters puts \(1/r_b\) in one over centimeters and the torque out by a factor of 100.
Filling down one row at a time in Part 2. The formulas alternate between two rows, so select both and drag them together.
Plotting \(\omega\) against the start or end time of its half turn. Every point slides sideways by half an interval, and the intervals shrink as the rotor speeds up, so the line tilts as well as shifts. \(\omega\) belongs at \(t_\text{MID}\).
A straight line through \(\theta\) against \(t\). The points curve upward, so the trendline is a polynomial of order 2, and \(\alpha\) is twice its \(t^2\) coefficient, not the coefficient itself.

title: Lab 8: Balanced and Unbalanced Torque
text:
Going deeper
Why the door handle is far from the hinges. Push a door right next to its hinges and it barely moves. Push at the handle and it swings. Torque is force times distance from the axle, so the same torque costs less force the farther out you push. Part 1 measures exactly that. Every time \(r_b\) doubles, \(F_T\) halves, because the product \(F_T r_b\) is fixed by the hanging mass on the other side. A seesaw works the same way, which is how a small child sitting far out can balance an adult sitting near the middle. The slope of the second graph is that fixed product.
Why the measured radius tends to come out a little large. The string pulls along its own centre line, not along the surface of the pipe, so the lever arm for the hanging mass is the pipe’s radius plus half the string’s thickness. A string 1 mm thick on a pipe of radius 16 mm adds 0.5 mm, which is about 3%. That is the same size as the example percent difference above. String wound over itself in layers adds more. So a positive percent difference of a few percent is what the string predicts, and a negative one points to another cause, such as friction in the axle or the caliper reading.
A free check on Part 2. Both Part 2 graphs carry the angular velocity at the first mark, \(\omega_0\). It is the intercept of \(\omega\) against \(t_\text{MID}\), and it is the coefficient of \(t\) in the polynomial fit of \(\theta\) against \(t\). In the example they are 0.93 rad/s and 0.91 rad/s. If yours disagree badly, look for a time typed into the wrong row.
What the two parts give together. If Part 2 used the same hanging mass on the same pipe, the torque spinning the rotor up is very close to the torque measured in Part 1. Close, not equal, because the falling mass accelerates, so the string pulls with \(M_H (g - \alpha r_a)\) rather than \(M_H g\). With the example numbers, \(\alpha r_a = (1.84\ \text{rad/s}^2)(0.0164\ \text{m}) = 0.030\ \text{m/s}^2\), about 0.3% of \(g\). Newton’s second law for rotation, \(\tau = I\alpha\), then gives the rotor’s moment of inertia \(I\), which is the rotational version of mass: how hard the rotor is to spin up, the way mass is how hard an object is to speed up. Here that is \(I = 0.0804 / 1.84 = 0.044\ \text{kg·m}^2\). Friction in the axle takes a little of the torque, and the slightly smaller string tension pushes the same way, so the true \(I\) is a little smaller.

text:
Most of the mathematics that gives physics students trouble is not hard. It is unmotivated. Somebody wrote \(\nabla \times \vect{B}\) on a board without ever saying what question a curl was invented to answer, and from that point on it is a symbol you manipulate rather than an idea you have.
These lessons go the other direction. Each one starts with a concrete problem somebody actually had, follows the reasoning that produced the tool, and only then writes down the notation.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text: Programming languages can feel like a mystical thing that doesn’t quite make sense. They are the opposite of that — they are purposeful and follow rigid, logical systems. This lesson is about where those systems come from, because once you can see the machinery, the syntax stops feeling arbitrary.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
What is a bit?
The term bit is short for binary digit. It is a system with two states, 0 or 1 — hence the “bi-” in binary.
If you are particularly inquisitive, you may ask: why 0 or 1? The answer is that it doesn’t really matter which two values we choose. Any two will do. The point is that we stay consistent. I have built circuits that look for two inputs, 0 V or 5 V, and that is still a binary system. We represent bits as 0 and 1 because of simplicity.

How are 0 and 1 simple?
The number 0 is associated with “nothing” or “off” in most people’s daily lives. 1 is clearly “not zero” — “not nothing,” “something.”
If I asked you “Is there a dog in your room?” and your answer was “no,” that corresponds to 0 dogs in your room. If your answer was “yes,” that corresponds to at least 1 dog being there. By this logic, 0 represents the absence of something and 1 represents the presence of something. That is the heart of a bit’s simplicity.
That same logic answers the next question you might have. Why binary? Why not trinary (0,1,2), or quaternary (0,1,2,3), or any other -nary you like? Again: simplicity. The simplest way I can think of to represent something is to ask whether it exists. No other details, just the very basic question — does it exist or not? Is there a dog in your room? No (0) or yes (1). There is almost no room for confusion, because both the question and the answer are extremely simple.
That simplicity matters enormously once we start building more complicated structures out of it.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
What is a bit, really?
Calling a bit a binary digit, or a system with two states, doesn’t actually tell us what a bit is. This is the genuinely fascinating part of the science underneath computers.
A bit is a single unit of information.
There is an entire field called Information Theory, which has been developing for roughly 160 years if you start the clock where I do. The accelerating advances in technology since around World War II run parallel to accelerating advances in this field. Some of you have heard of quantum computers relying on qubits without realising that a qubit is simply the quantum version of a bit, used in Quantum Information Theory.
Without going into a full history: in 1867, James Clerk Maxwell was trying to poke holes in the second law of thermodynamics — the one saying entropy always increases in a closed system — and came up with a logic test for it. His thought experiment, Maxwell’s Demon, is still somewhat relevant today. It has been solved. Probably. But it persists in some ways.
The pursuit of resolving Maxwell’s Demon eventually led to a realisation: information is a real, physical quantity. Just as you measure your height in feet, inches, and centimetres, information is measured in bits.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
Representing information with bits
To exchange or store information, we need a way to represent it.
Picture someone using a flashlight to transmit a message in Morse code. The photons coming out of that flashlight have no special property that lets them carry information. And yet an exchange of information happens, because we encode the message into the existence and nonexistence of those photons. One level deeper, the encoding is actually tied to a change in the entropy of the system — more on that in a moment.
Let’s represent the flashlight being off as 0 and on as 1, and take the simplest possible case where a single bit equals a single unit of Morse code time. Here is how a message might look1:
010100000001011101010001110111011100010101011100010000000111010111000101110001011101000101110001110111011100011101011100010
That translates to “I love karaoke.” I started and ended the message with a 0 to account for the information associated with having no signal at the beginning and the end. Sent this way, the message took 123 bits.
Does that mean the information that I, personally, love karaoke has a physical size of 123 bits? No, not really. The message “I love karaoke” is what we encoded in 123 bits — not the information of what any of that means. It is important here to separate your colloquial sense of “information” as the meaning of something from the scientific definition.
The 123 bits I used could easily have been 121 by leaving off the bordering zeros. It could have been 200 if I added more, or if I picked a different representation scheme altogether. Morse himself designed Morse code so that common letters take less time, which is why common letters tend to be built out of dots — a dot costs 1 bit here and a dash costs 3. Rearrange the scheme and the same message might take 500 bits, or 50.
The bits do not hold some grandiose, obscure meaning. The information is contained in ordering the bits the specific way we chose. If I send the word “love” to 100 people, it may mean 100 different things to them. The information carried by the bits is not the meaning of the word love. It is specifically just the word love.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
Information is negative entropy
In the early days of resolving Maxwell’s Demon, Leo Szilard developed the idea that knowledge is associated with a dissolution of entropy. Knowledge, and information, become intrinsically related to the energy required to reduce the entropy of a system.
Entropy is a measure of the order or disorder of a system. One useful way to think about it is how likely a system is to exist by pure randomness.
Flip 30 water bottles. If all 30 land perfectly upside down on their caps, that final arrangement is a very low entropy system — it is an extremely unlikely outcome. If only a few land on their caps, which is far more likely, it is a high entropy system. More naturally-random results means more entropy.
Here is the interesting part. You can arrange those 30 bottles by hand, exactly as if they had all been perfectly cap-flipped, and the final system has the same low-entropy state as the one that got there by chance. Either way, there is an energy cost associated with taking the bottles from a high entropy state (more likely to exist) to a low entropy state (less likely to exist).
The information carried by a flashing flashlight arises from arranging those flashes in one specific way. It is not really the bits themselves that contain the information — it is the change in entropy away from the likely, more random state. Storing or communicating information explicitly requires forcing a system into a lower entropy state, and it is that state which holds the information. The bits are just how we represent it.

These same logical sequences are the exact tenets that created programming languages. Your computer “thinks” by manipulating bits and gates, and programming languages were devised as a way for you to do that manipulation without wiring anything.
This is why I think anyone diving into programming should understand a little about information theory and computers. Code is not a mystical thing that refuses to make sense. It is the opposite — rigid, purposeful, logical systems all the way down.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
Memory
Now extend the idea that information is a physical quantity.
In the flashlight example, each bit erases the state of the one before it. But what if we could store whether a switch was on or off? Say we have 123 physical switches. We set them into the positions of that message, leave them there, and go do something else. When we come back, the bits are still where we left them.
That ability to store information rather than merely transmit it is memory.
Memory hardware has advanced enormously in the last thirty years, but the principle has not changed: to store information, even temporarily, you need a physical way to contain it. This is one of the real physical limits of a computer, and it is exactly why you cannot just download more RAM.
RAM (Random Access Memory) is very fast memory designed to hold things temporarily. It is the quick-access memory your programs actually live in, and it will usually be the limiting component when you are programming. Cut the power and it is gone.
HDD (Hard Disk Drive), now quickly becoming obsolete, uses a spinning metal platter and a little magnetic arm to literally write bits onto the disk.
SSD (Solid State Drive) is much faster because nothing moves. Instead of magnets it uses microscopic floating-gate transistors, which physically trap electrons in a specific pattern and hold that pattern even with the power off.
Anything you do on a computer uses memory.

title: How Computers Actually Work
text:
CPU and GPU
There is also a limit on how fast a processor can move that information around, though it is usually less of a roadblock than memory.
The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is typically very fast at single, sequential tasks. Say you write a program teaching the computer to do a kickflip. To do a kickflip it first has to learn what a kickflip is, then what a skateboard is, then how to ride one, then how to ollie, then how to kickflip, and then actually do it. A CPU rips through steps like that.
What it is not so fast at is doing many things at once. If you knew exactly how to paint every part of a picture, a CPU would still go paint every individual part of it, spot by spot, with one brush.
The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is where that changes. A GPU is slower at any single task, but it can do enormous numbers of them simultaneously. Give it the same painting and it picks up 5,000 brushes and paints every spot at once — vastly faster than one brush going spot to spot.
The trade-off runs the other way too. The GPU is much slower at learning to do the kickflip, because all those sequential steps still have to happen first, and it relies on the CPU to tell it what it is supposed to be painting in the first place.
